newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed to visit NATO military nerve centre.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed to visit NATO military nerve centre.

text.p: Russian security supremo Alexander Lebed meets senior commanders at the nerve centre of NATO's military machine on Tuesday after voicing reluctant acceptance of alliance plans for eastwards expansion.
On the second day of his first trip to the West, Lebed, an ex-paratroop general, will visit NATO's military headquarters at Mons in southern Belgium for talks on Bosnia.

The gravel-voiced reserve paratroop general, a strong candidate to succeed President Boris Yeltsin if he has to bow out of office due to ill health, will visit the operations' room of the alliance-led peace mission in Bosnia.
Lebed, who is Yeltsin's security adviser, will discuss Russia's continued participation in the force if its mandate is extended next year.
On Monday, Lebed voiced grudging acceptance of NATO's plans to enlarge eastwards to take in some of Moscow's former satellites in eastern and central Europe.
"Whatever NATO decides, Russia is not going to go into hysterics," the 46-year-old Lebed told a news conference.
But Lebed left the door open to future discussion on NATO's relationship with Russia and the issue of expansion.

"We are all products, victims of the Cold War, we are not going to solve these problems in 24 hours," Lebed said after meeting with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and the ambassadors of the alliance's 16 member states.

Russia has tried to link enlargement with a new treaty or charter governing all relations between the two former Cold War foes. It sees expansion as a threat to its security. NATO rejects any idea of linkage.
Lebed said he accepted NATO's right to expand if it wished but said the problem was one of timing. "The main thing is not to hurry, or you may trip up," Lebed said.
NATO intends next year to invite countries to open entry talks with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic as the most likely candidates.
Some NATO diplomats interpreted Lebed's words as a signal that Moscow considered enlargement inevitable.
"He, above all, insisted on the question of timing as if the principle was now non-negotiable," said one ambassador.
A senior diplomat described Lebed as a highly intelligent man in a rational "listening mode". There was, he said, no "over-the-top language".
"We are enormously encouraged...We see him as a very important figure whatever the future holds," the official said.
The ambassador of one applicant country said he found Lebed's views "very interesting".
"I think he wants to deal. The question is: Will the others allow him to do so ?," he told Reuters.
Western officials were clearly eager to gain a first-hand impression of the man who performed so strongly in elections this year.
